items.label: text
items.text: We met ionic compounds in Chapter 7 and in this chapter we will understand what covalent bonding is. There are a lot more covalent compounds than ionic compounds so it is important that you understand how the bonding works.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 8.1 Water is a covalent compound but the salt dissolved in sea water is an ionic compound.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know that a covalent bond is formed between atoms by the sharing of a pair of electrons

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand covalent bonds in terms of electrostatic attractions

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand how to use dot-and-cross diagrams to represent covalent bonds in:

items.label: list_item
items.text: diatomic molecules, including hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, halogens and hydrogen halides

items.label: list_item
items.text: inorganic molecules, including water, ammonia and carbon dioxide

items.label: list_item
items.text: organic molecules containing up to two carbon atoms, including methane, ethane, ethene and those containing halogen atoms

items.label: list_item
items.text: Explain why substances with a simple molecular structure are gases or liquids, or solids with low melting and boiling points

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand that the term intermolecular forces of attraction can be used to represent all forces between molecules

items.label: list_item
items.text: Explain why the melting and boiling points of substances with simple molecular structures increase, in general, with increasing relative molecular mass

items.label: list_item
items.text: Explain why substances with giant covalent structures are solids with high melting and boiling points

items.label: list_item
items.text: Explain how the structures of diamond, graphite and C6o fullerene influence their physical properties, including electrical conductivity and hardness

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know that covalent compounds do not usually conduct electricity

items.label: text
items.text: In any bond, particles are held together by electrostatic attractions between something positively charged and something negatively charged. In a covalent bond, a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms. What holds the atoms together is the strong electrostatic attraction between the nuclei (positively charged) of the atoms that make up the bond, and the shared pair of electrons (negatively charged).
